units.title: C1 The particulate nature of matter

topics.title: C1.1 The particulate nature of matter

outcomes.text: Name the distinguishing properties of solids, liquids and gases.
Describe how particles are spaced, arranged and moving in each state.
Explain changes of state using kinetic particle theory and energy changes.
Describe and explain diffusion as movement of particles.
Explain how the rate of diffusion depends on molecular mass.
Name suitable apparatus for measuring time, temperature, mass and volume, including burettes, pipettes and measuring cylinders.
Read simple chromatograms.
Read chromatograms and use Rf values.
Explain how locating agents let chromatography work on colourless substances.
Recognise that mixtures melt and boil over a range of temperatures.
Judge a substance's identity and purity from melting and boiling points.
Describe and explain solvent use, filtration, crystallisation, distillation, fractional distillation and paper chromatography.
Choose suitable separation techniques given information about the substances.
Identify physical and chemical changes and explain how they differ.
Describe how elements, mixtures and compounds differ, and how metals differ from non-metals.
Define solvent, solute, solution and concentration.

topics.title: C3.3 Atomic structure and the Periodic Table

outcomes.text: Describe an atom as a nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electron shells.
Describe how electrons fill shells and why noble gas structures and outer electrons matter.
Give the relative charge and approximate mass of protons, neutrons and electrons.
Define and use proton (atomic) number.
Define and use nucleon (mass) number.
Use proton number and atomic structure to explain the Periodic Table for elements 1 to 20.
Define isotopes as atoms with the same proton number but different nucleon number.
Explain why isotopes of an element have the same properties: same outer-shell electrons.
Describe how ions form by gaining or losing electrons.
Use dot-and-cross diagrams for ionic bonds between Group I and Group VII.
Describe ionic bond formation between metals and non-metals, with strong attraction between opposite charges.
Describe the ionic lattice as alternating positive and negative ions, as in sodium chloride.
State that non-metals form simple molecules with covalent bonds.
Describe single covalent bonds in H2, Cl2, H2O, CH4, NH3 and HCl as shared electron pairs, using dot-and-cross diagrams.
Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for N2, C2H4, CH3OH and CO2.
Compare volatility, solubility and conductivity of ionic and covalent compounds.
Explain melting and boiling point differences between ionic and covalent compounds using attractive forces.
State that carbon has several forms, including diamond and graphite.
Describe the giant covalent structures of diamond and graphite.
Link the structures of diamond and graphite to their uses.
Use element symbols and write formulae of simple compounds.
Work out the formula of an ionic compound from the ion charges.
Work out a simple compound's formula from the numbers of atoms present.
Work out a simple compound's formula from a model or diagram.
Write and use word equations.
Interpret and balance simple symbol equations.
Write symbol equations with state symbols, including ionic equations.
Deduce a balanced equation from given information.
Define relative atomic mass Ar using the carbon-12 scale.
Define relative molecular (formula) mass Mr and calculate it from Ar values.
Calculate reacting masses, gas volumes and solution volumes, and concentrations in g/dm3 and mol/dm3, including limiting reactants.
Define electrolysis as breaking down a molten or dissolved ionic compound with electricity.
Use the terms inert electrode, electrolyte, anode and cathode.
Explain electrolysis through the ions present and electrode reactions: cations gain, anions lose electrons.
Describe electrode products and observations in electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide, concentrated aqueous sodium chloride and dilute sulfuric acid.
Predict the products of electrolysing a molten binary compound.

units.title: C6 Energy changes in chemical reactions

outcomes.text: Describe exothermic and endothermic reactions.
Describe bond breaking as endothermic and bond forming as exothermic.
Draw and label energy level diagrams from data.
Interpret energy level diagrams, including activation energy.
Describe the thermal energy released when fuels burn.
State hydrogen's use as a fuel.
Describe practical ways to study the rate of a gas-producing reaction.
Interpret rate-of-reaction experimental data.
Describe how concentration, particle size, catalysts and temperature affect rate.
Explain the concentration effect through collision frequency.
Explain the temperature effect through collision frequency and more particles having activation energy.
Describe how concentration, temperature and surface area create explosion danger in fine powders and gases.
Describe oxidation and reduction as oxygen gain or loss.
Define and identify oxidising and reducing agents.

topics.title: C7.1 The characteristic properties of acids and bases

outcomes.text: Describe acid properties, including effects on litmus and reactions with metals, bases and carbonates.
Describe base properties, including litmus effect and reactions with acids and ammonium salts.
Define acids and bases by proton transfer in aqueous solution.
Describe neutrality, acidity and alkalinity using pH and universal indicator.
Describe and explain why controlling soil acidity matters.
Classify oxides as acidic or basic from metallic or non-metallic character.
Identify neutral and amphoteric oxides.
Describe preparing, separating and purifying salts using the C2 techniques and C7.1 reactions.
Suggest a method for making a given salt, including precipitation.

topics.title: C7.4 Identification of ions and gases

outcomes.text: Describe and use tests for aqueous cations, flame tests, anions and the common gases.
Describe the Periodic Table as a way to classify elements and predict properties.
Describe the change from metallic to non-metallic character across a period.
Explain how group number, outer electrons and metallic character are related.
Describe lithium, sodium and potassium as soft metals with trends in melting point, density and reaction with water.
Predict properties of other Group I elements from data.
Describe chlorine, bromine and iodine as diatomic non-metals with trends in colour and state.
State how halogens react with other halide ions.
Predict properties of other Group VII elements from data.
Identify trends in other groups from data.
Describe transition elements: dense, high melting points, coloured compounds, often catalysts.
Describe noble gases as unreactive monoatomic gases and explain this using electronic structure.
State uses of noble gases for inert atmospheres, such as argon lamps and helium balloons.
Describe the general physical properties of metals.
Describe metallic bonding as positive ions in a sea of electrons and use it to explain conductivity and malleability.
Describe alloys, such as brass, as mixtures of a metal with other elements.
Explain why alloys are used instead of pure metals.
Describe how additives change iron into steels such as mild and stainless steel.
Order potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron and copper by their reactions with water, acid and carbon.
Describe the reactivity series as the tendency to form positive ions, shown by displacement reactions.
Deduce an order of reactivity from experimental results.
Describe using carbon to extract some metals from their ores.
Know that aluminium is extracted from bauxite by electrolysis.
Describe and explain the main reactions in the blast furnace extraction of iron.
Describe uses of aluminium in aircraft parts and food containers.
Explain aluminium's apparent unreactivity through its oxide layer.
State uses of mild steel and stainless steel.
Explain zinc's use in galvanising steel and making brass.
Describe chemical tests for water using copper(II) sulfate and cobalt(II) chloride.
Describe how hydration can be reversed by heating.
Describe and explain water supply treatment by filtration and chlorination.
State the composition of clean air.
Name the common air pollutants: carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
State the source of each pollutant.
Describe ways to reduce sulfur dioxide emissions.
Describe how a catalytic converter removes nitrogen monoxide and carbon monoxide.
State the harmful effects of these pollutants on buildings and health.
State the conditions needed for iron to rust.
Describe and explain barrier methods of rust prevention.
Describe and explain sacrificial protection and galvanising.
State how carbon dioxide forms in combustion, respiration, acid-carbonate reactions and thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate.
State that carbon dioxide and methane are greenhouse gases.
Describe making lime from limestone and uses of limestone in treating acidic soil and waste.
Describe the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate.
Name and draw methane, ethane, ethene and ethanol.
State the compound type from a name ending -ane, -ene or -ol, or from a structure.
State that coal, natural gas and petroleum are fossil fuels producing carbon dioxide when burned.
Name methane as the main constituent of natural gas.
Describe petroleum as a hydrocarbon mixture separated by fractional distillation.
Describe the properties of molecules within a fraction.
Name the uses of the fractions.
Describe alkanes and alkenes as families with a general formula and similar chemical properties.
Describe alkanes as saturated hydrocarbons with only single covalent bonds.
Describe alkanes as generally unreactive except for burning.
Describe complete combustion of hydrocarbons to carbon dioxide and water.
Describe alkenes as unsaturated hydrocarbons with one double bond.
State that cracking produces alkenes.
Describe cracking of large alkanes into smaller alkanes, alkenes and hydrogen, and the conditions.
Recognise saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons from structure and bromine water.
Describe addition reactions of alkenes with bromine, hydrogen and steam.
Describe forming poly(ethene) by addition polymerisation.
State that ethanol forms by fermentation and by ethene reacting with steam.
Describe ethanol formation by fermentation and catalytic addition of steam to ethene.
Describe complete combustion of ethanol.
State uses of ethanol as a solvent and fuel.
Use rules and measuring cylinders to find length or volume.
Understand that a micrometer screw gauge measures very small distances.
Use analogue and digital clocks to measure time intervals.
Average small distances and short times by measuring multiples, including a pendulum period.
Define speed and calculate average speed.
Distinguish speed from velocity.
Define and calculate acceleration from change in velocity.
Plot and interpret speed-time and distance-time graphs.
Calculate acceleration from the gradient of a speed-time graph.
Recognise rest, constant speed and changing speed from graph shape.
Recognise linear motion with non-constant acceleration.
Calculate distance from the area under a speed-time graph.
Relate acceleration and deceleration to changing speed using graph gradient.
State that free-fall acceleration g near Earth is constant.
Describe falling with and without air resistance, including terminal velocity.
Show familiarity with the idea of mass.
Understand that mass resists changes in motion.
Understand that weights (and masses) can be compared on a balance.
State that weight is a gravitational force.
Distinguish between mass and weight.
Describe weight as the effect of a gravitational field on a mass.
Recognise g as force on unit mass, in N/kg, and use W = mg.
Recall and use density = mass / volume.
Describe an experiment to find the density of a liquid or regular solid.
Find the density of an irregular solid by displacement.
Recognise that a force can change size, shape or motion.
Plot and interpret extension-load graphs and describe the procedure.
State Hooke's law and use F = kx.
Recognise the limit of proportionality on an extension-load graph.
Use F = ma linking resultant force, mass and acceleration.
Understand friction as a force between surfaces that impedes motion and heats.
Recognise air resistance as friction.
Find the resultant of forces acting along the same line.
Recognise that with no resultant force a body stays at rest or keeps constant speed in a straight line.
Describe a moment as a force's turning effect, with everyday examples.
Calculate moment as force times perpendicular distance from the pivot.
Apply the principle of moments to a balanced weightless beam.
Recognise equilibrium when there is no resultant force or turning effect.
Perform an experiment to find the centre of mass of a plane lamina.
Describe how centre of mass position affects stability.
Relate pressure qualitatively to force and area.
Recall and use p = F / A.
Relate work done to force and distance moved, without calculation.
Recall and use W = Fd = change in energy.
Understand that work done equals energy transferred.
Understand that objects have kinetic or potential energy, and energy can be transferred and stored.
Give examples of changes between kinetic, gravitational, chemical, elastic, nuclear and thermal energy.
Recall and use KE = 1/2 mv2 and GPE = mgh.
Recognise transfer by forces, electric currents, heating and waves.
Apply conservation of energy to simple examples.
Relate power to work done and time, without calculation.
Recall and use P = change in E / t.
Distinguish renewable from non-renewable energy sources.
Describe how energy is obtained from fuels, water, geothermal, nuclear fission, solar and wind.
Give advantages and disadvantages of each method.
Understand the Sun is the source of all resources except geothermal, nuclear and tidal.
Understand tidal energy mainly comes from the moon.
Show understanding that nuclear fusion releases energy in the Sun.
Show qualitative understanding of efficiency.
Recall and use the efficiency equations for energy and power.

topics.title: P2.1.1 Thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases

outcomes.text: State the distinguishing properties of solids, liquids and gases.
Describe the molecular structure of solids, liquids and gases.
Describe gas pressure and temperature in terms of particle motion.
Describe thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases at constant pressure.
Explain everyday uses and consequences of expansion.
Know the relative size of expansion in solids, liquids and gases.
Describe how a temperature-dependent property can measure temperature.
Understand sensitivity, range and linearity.
Recognise the need for fixed points.
Describe how liquid-in-glass thermometers work.
Use thermometers on the Celsius scale.
Describe a thermocouple and its use for high or rapidly changing temperatures.
Describe melting and boiling as energy input without temperature change.
State melting and boiling point meanings and the values for water.
Distinguish boiling from evaporation.
Name typical good and bad thermal conductors.
Describe experiments comparing thermal conductors.
Explain conduction through molecular vibrations and electron transfer.
Recognise convection as the main energy transfer in fluids.
Relate convection to density changes.
Interpret experiments illustrating convection in liquids and gases.
Recognise radiation as energy transfer needing no medium.
Identify infrared as the radiation involved in energy transfer.
Describe how surface colour and texture affect emission, absorption and reflection.
Interpret experiments on good and bad emitters and absorbers of infrared.
Explain everyday applications and consequences of conduction, convection and radiation.

units.title: P3 Properties of waves, including light and sound

outcomes.text: Understand that waves transfer energy without transferring matter.
Describe wave motion using ropes, springs and water waves.
Use the term wavefront.
State the meaning of speed, frequency, wavelength and amplitude.
Distinguish transverse from longitudinal waves with examples.
Describe reflection at a plane surface and refraction from speed change.
Use water waves to demonstrate reflection and refraction.
Recall and use v = f x wavelength.
Understand refraction as caused by a change of speed between media.
Describe diffraction through a narrow gap, shown with water waves.
Describe image formation by a plane mirror and its characteristics.
Recall and use angle of incidence = angle of reflection, measured to the normal.
Do simple constructions and calculations for plane mirror reflection.
Recall that a plane mirror image is virtual.
Give the meaning of critical angle.
Describe internal and total internal reflection.
Describe how optical fibres work, in medicine and communications.
Describe an experiment showing refraction of light.
Use the terms angle of incidence and refraction, and describe light through parallel-sided material.
Recall and use the definition of refractive index in terms of speed.
Recall and use n = sin i / sin r.
Describe how a thin converging lens acts on a light beam.
Use the terms principal focus and focal length.
Draw ray diagrams for a real image by a single lens.
Understand real and virtual images.
Draw ray diagrams for a virtual image by a converging lens.
Describe images as enlarged, same size or diminished, and upright or inverted.
Describe using a single lens as a magnifying glass.
Describe the electromagnetic spectrum in order of frequency, from radio waves to gamma rays.
State that all electromagnetic waves travel at the same high speed in a vacuum.
State that this speed is 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, about the same in air.
Describe properties and uses of radiation in each region, including radio, microwaves, infrared and X-rays.
Describe how vibrating objects make sound and how sound makes objects, such as the eardrum, vibrate.
Describe the longitudinal nature of sound waves.
Describe sound in air through compressions and rarefactions.
State the audible frequency range of 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.
Show understanding that sound needs a medium.
Describe forces between magnets, and between magnets and magnetic materials.
Give an account of induced magnetism.
Distinguish magnetic from non-magnetic materials.
Draw and describe the field lines around a bar magnet.
Distinguish magnetic properties of soft iron and steel.
Recognise that an electric current has a magnetic field.
Distinguish permanent magnets from electromagnets in design and use.
Describe magnetisation by stroking, d.c. in a coil and hammering.
Describe demagnetisation by hammering, heating and a.c. in a coil.
State that there are positive and negative charges.
State that unlike charges attract and like charges repel.
Describe experiments producing and detecting charge by friction.
State that charging adds or removes electrons.
Describe an electric field as a region where a charge feels a force.
Distinguish conductors from insulators with examples.
State that current is related to flow of charge.
Understand current as rate of flow of charge and use I = Q/t.
Distinguish electron flow from conventional current.
Use and describe analogue and digital ammeters.
State that current in metals is a flow of electrons.

topics.title: P4.2.3 Electromotive force (e.m.f.) and potential difference (p.d.)

outcomes.text: State that p.d. across a component is measured in volts.
Understand e.m.f. as energy supplied by a source driving charge round a circuit.
Use and describe analogue and digital voltmeters.
State that e.m.f. is measured in volts.
Recall that 1 V is equivalent to 1 J/C.
State resistance = p.d. / current and understand how changes in p.d. or resistance affect current.
Recall and use R = V / I.
Describe an experiment to find resistance with a voltmeter and ammeter.
Relate wire resistance to length and diameter without calculation.
Understand current, p.d., e.m.f. and resistance together.
Use proportionality of resistance to length and inverse proportionality to cross-sectional area.
Draw and interpret circuit diagrams with sources, switches, resistors, lamps, ammeters, voltmeters and fuses.
Understand that current is the same at every point in a series circuit.
Calculate combined resistance of resistors in series.
Use that p.d.s across series components sum to the supply p.d.
State that source current is larger than the current in each parallel branch.
Use that source current equals the sum of branch currents.
State that two resistors in parallel have less combined resistance than either alone.
Calculate combined resistance of two resistors in parallel.
State the advantages of parallel connection.
Draw and interpret circuits with NTC thermistors and LDRs.
Describe how NTC thermistors and LDRs act as input transducers.
Recall and use P = IV and E = IVt.
State the hazards of damaged insulation, overheated cables and damp conditions.
State that a fuse protects a circuit.
Explain fuses and circuit breakers and choose suitable ratings.
Explain the benefits of earthing metal cases.
Understand that a moving conductor or changing magnetic field can induce an e.m.f.
Describe an experiment demonstrating electromagnetic induction.
State the factors affecting the size of an induced e.m.f.
Understand that the induced e.m.f. direction opposes the change causing it.
Distinguish direct from alternating current.
Describe and explain a rotating-coil generator and slip rings.
Sketch a voltage-time graph for a simple a.c. generator.
Describe the construction of a basic transformer with a soft-iron core.
Describe the principle of transformer operation.
Use the terms step-up and step-down.
Recall and use Vp/Vs = Np/Ns (100% efficiency).
Recall and use IpVp = IsVs (100% efficiency).
Describe transformers in high-voltage electricity transmission.
Explain why cable power losses are lower at high voltage.

topics.title: P4.6.4 Force on a current-carrying conductor

outcomes.text: Describe an experiment showing a force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, including reversing current and field.
State that a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field turns, more with extra turns, current or field strength.
Relate the turning effect to an electric motor with a split-ring commutator.
Describe the nucleus as protons and neutrons.
Use the terms proton number Z and nucleon number A.
Use and interpret nuclide notation.
Use and explain the term isotope.
Demonstrate understanding of background radiation.
Describe detecting alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays.

topics.title: P5.2.2 Characteristics of the three kinds of emission

outcomes.text: Describe the random nature of radioactive emission.
Identify alpha, beta and gamma by nature, ionising effect and penetrating ability.
Describe their deflection in electric and magnetic fields.
Give and explain practical applications of each emission.
State the meaning of radioactive decay.
Use word equations for nuclear changes when particles are emitted.
Use nuclide notation to show the effect of alpha and beta decay.
Show understanding of half-life and use the term in context.
Use half-life in simple calculations from tables or decay curves.
Calculate half-life from data or decay curves, including unsubtracted background radiation.
Recall the effects of ionising radiation on living things.
Describe safe handling, use and storage of radioactive materials.
